key_insight: The paper shows that sequential shift detection in unstructured AI data can stay statistically valid even when the detector adaptively learns what kind of shift to look for.
clinical_relevance: For clinical AI systems such as AI scribes, this could enable faster and more reliable detection of distribution shifts that may affect system behavior, safety, or downstream workflow quality.
method: Reframes changepoint detection as a testing-by-betting game with an adaptive witness function.
Introduces asymptotic e-detectors that use a calibration set to approximate the pre-change distribution and control false alarms as calibration size grows.
Builds both black-box embedding-based bettors and interpretable LLM-concept bettors for monitoring unstructured data.
evidence_signal: Across three real-world datasets, including a clinical AI scribe deployment, the adaptive monitors detected shifts faster than fixed monitors at the same false-alarm level, and calibration sets as small as 30 were effective.
watch_item: The strongest formal false-alarm guarantees are asymptotic and depend on calibration data quality and whether the observed shift is well captured by the learned witness function.
paper_title: Learning to Detect Shifts in Unstructured Data Streams via Monitoring-by-Betting
